To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) we developed a novel multiobjective calibration approach to simulate both water column temperature (R2 = 0.99, RMSE = 0.3°C) and water column stratification (R2 =.62) and (b) we found that the artificial circulation deployed in our study area was not sufficient to significantly reduce the ability of the buoyant cyanobacterial taxa to outcompete the nonbuoyant algal taxa.

(1) a 1D turbulent diffusion model with artificial circulation term can realistically simulate water column temperature and stratification in a eutrophic reservoir; (2) the implemented artificial circulation rate in our study area has minimal influence on cyanobacteria light limitation; and (3) the proposed multi objective calibration approach provides a more robust calibration than single objective calibration approaches.

(1) the multi objective approach we developed for calibrating the 1D model provides realistic estimates of water temperature and stability, (2) artificial circulation in our study area is insufficient to substantially alter vertical mixing, and (3), in our study area, artificial mixing at the implemented rate would be insufficient to substantially reduce the potential for cyanobacteria blooms
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development and implementation of a novel multiobjective calibration approach to simulate water temperature and stability using a one-dimensional (1D) hydrodynamic model in a shallow turbid reservoir.
the development and application of an efficient and systematic method for characterizing the vertical diffusion in shallow turbid lakes.
the development of a parsimonious 1D turbulent diffusion model with the capability to simulate the impact of artificial circulators on vertical mixing.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

our study demonstrates an efficient approach to characterizing vertical mixing and its impact of cyanobacteria bloom dynamics in shallow lakes and reservoirs and that the approach is applicable to a wide variety of lakes and reservoirs with different circulation regimes.

this study demonstrates an approach for characterizing mixing and cyanobacteria light competition in shallow lakes and reservoirs that could be applied to other systems to inform management decisions.

the study demonstrates the potential of a novel multi objective 1D turbulent diffusion model to realistically simulate both vertical mixing and water temperature, which can be applied to a wide range of lakes and reservoirs to assess the potential of artificial circulation to mitigate cyanobacteria blooms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the artificial circulation implemented in the study reservoir had minimal effect on water column stability and therefore cyanobacteria bloom dynamics, suggesting that artificial mixing may not be an effective tool to reduce cyanobacteria dominance and associated harmful algal blooms (HABs) in shallow turbid lakes and reservoirs.

the vertical mixing in our study system is insufficient to substantially reduce cyanobacteria dominance and thus, that artificial circulators may not be a viable option for mitigating cyanobacteria blooms in this system.

the vertical diffusion model with artificial circulation term is a useful tool to assess mixing in shallow eutrophic systems and to explore the impact of mixing on cyanobacteria light limitation relative to other al gal groups.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the implementation of artificial mixing to control cyanobacteria dominance is unlikely to be effective in turbid, shallow lakes and reservoirs with high wind speeds and high nutrient loading.
artificial circulation may be ineffective in shallow turbid systems, and other approaches such as biomanipulation should be considered.
the potential for artificial circulation to reduce cyanobacteria blooms in shallow turbid reservoirs may be limited.
